The founder

Hi, I'm Nourie.

My grandpa has run this farm for years. I grew up around it without thinking much about it — until I got interested in nutrition and wellness, and started asking where food actually comes from.

That question led me back to his farm. At 16, I took over a small piece of it and started growing hydroponically: no soil, just nutrient-rich water and a lot of trial and error.

"I started by talking about food. Then I wanted to understand it. Then I started growing it."

I've gotten good at noticing when something's off — a plant growing slower than it should, aphids showing up somewhere they shouldn't. Instead of reaching for a pesticide, I bring in the bug that actually eats the problem.

The farm is still growing. So am I.

The good bugs

No pesticide sprays.
So what do we do about bugs?

We get other bugs.

It's called biological pest control: every pest has a natural predator, so instead of spraying, we introduce that predator and let it do the hunting. I scout the plants for early signs of pests, then bring in the insect that actually eats that pest — the population stays balanced without a single chemical spray.

Field notes: figuring out what's eating what

Ladybugs

Aphids cluster on new growth and drain the plant's sap. One ladybug can eat dozens a day.

Lacewings

The larvae do the real work, hunting down aphids and mites long before they grow wings.

Predatory Mites

Too small to see with the eye, so we check for them under the microscope instead.

Parasitic Wasps

They lay eggs inside pest insects, stopping an outbreak before it starts.

The systems

Three ways we grow

For the leafy stuff

NFT — Nutrient Film Technique

A thin stream of nutrient water runs past the roots, nonstop. This is where our lettuce and chard grow.

For the bigger stuff

Dutch Buckets

Bigger plants get their own bucket and supply line — tomatoes and cucumbers grow here.

The original way

Soil

Not everything is hydroponic — some of the farm is still grown the regular way, straight in the ground.
